title: When High Performance Suffocates a Career
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Describes an ironic career trap: high performers become so valuable in a narrow role that the organization keeps them there rather than promoting them, because no one else can replace them. The competence that should open doors instead locks them in place, since promotion would create a gap the organization can't easily fill. The piece's prescribed exit strategy is for the high performer to document their process, delegate portions of it, actively seek stretch assignments that build new skills, and, as a last resort, explore external opportunities to force the organization's hand.
points: High performers can become invisible in the promotion process precisely because they're too valuable to move out of their current role.
The escape route starts with documenting the work and training a backfill, deliberately making oneself less indispensable in the current seat.
Signaling appetite for new challenges through small stretch assignments, and as a last resort exploring outside opportunities, forces organizations to confront the cost of keeping talent stuck.
quotes: In an odd irony, their competence and high performance make them more valuable to the organization right where they are. Which is exactly the problem.
Over time, they do the job so well that they become invisible in the promotion process.
To escape this trap, these high performers must coach and mentor others to do what they do and at the same level, thus replacing themselves by design.
Once a “backfill” candidate exists or is in process, the high performer’s next move is to seek assignments and projects that help them develop new competencies and skills.
As a last resort, high performers trapped in place by their own competence should explore opportunities outside the team or organization.
When a team member is too valuable to move up, they are also too valuable to move on.
